title: Valid Palindrome: left/right skipping non-alphanumeric.
shortTitle: Valid Palindrome: Left/Right Pointers Skipping Non-Alphanumeric
keyPoints: Use two pointers closing in from both ends of the string, one from the left and one from the right.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters using Character.isLetterOrDigit before comparing.
Compare characters case-insensitively using Character.toLowerCase on both sides.
Guard inner skip loops with the same left < right condition to prevent pointers from crossing.
An empty string or a string of only punctuation is considered a valid palindrome.
This approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, avoiding the allocation of a cleaned or reversed copy.
Avoid the naive strip-and-reverse approach which uses O(n) extra space unnecessarily.

s1_definition.oneliner: Two pointers close in from both ends, skip non-alphanumeric characters, compare lowercased letters, and declare a palindrome if they meet without a mismatch.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Valid palindrome check** – determines whether a string reads the same forward and backward after ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and treating letters case-insensitively.
- **Opposite-end two pointers** – a `left` pointer starts at position 0 and a `right` pointer starts at the last position, moving toward each other.
- **Skip non-alphanumeric** – each pointer advances past characters where `Character.isLetterOrDigit` returns false before comparing.
- **Case-insensitive comparison** – `Character.toLowerCase` is applied to both characters before checking equality.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space** – each character is examined at most once, and no extra string is allocated.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, printed reference codes contain dashes and spaces for readability, but an internal checksum rule requires the alphanumeric core to be symmetric. Rajesh reads from both ends toward the middle, skipping any dash or space, and checks that each matching pair of real characters is the same letter or digit regardless of case.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Two-pointer palindrome check:

  Input: "N B I - 1 2 1 - I B N"
          ^                     ^
         left                 right

  Step 1: Both on alphanumeric
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ left='N', right='N'                 │
  │ toLowerCase: 'n' == 'n' -> match    │
  │ Move both inward                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Step 2: Skip spaces, land on next
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ left='B', right='B'                 │
  │ toLowerCase: 'b' == 'b' -> match    │
  │ Move both inward                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Step 3: Skip spaces
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ left='I', right='I'                 │
  │ toLowerCase: 'i' == 'i' -> match    │
  │ Move both inward                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Step 4: Skip dashes
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ left='1', right='1'                 │
  │ '1' == '1' -> match                 │
  │ Move both inward                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Step 5: Pointers meet at center
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ left='2', right='2' (same index)    │
  │ left < right is false -> exit loop  │
  │ Return TRUE: valid palindrome       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Pointer movement:

  N   B   I   -   1   2   1   -   I   B   N
  ^                                       ^
  L→  →   →   skip →   ←   skip  ←   ←  ←R
              ───▶           ◀───
           pointers meet in center
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Palindrome checks whether a string reads the same forward and backward once you ignore everything that is not a letter or digit and treat letters case-insensitively. The two-pointer approach solves this in O(n) time and O(1) space by working directly on the original string. A left pointer starts at the front and a right pointer starts at the back, each skipping non-alphanumeric characters before comparing the lowercased values.

The critical correctness detail is guarding the inner skip loops with the same `left < right` condition as the outer loop. Without that guard, the pointers can cross each other while skipping punctuation, causing out-of-bounds reads. This guard also makes strings that are entirely punctuation or empty come out as valid palindromes, because the pointers simply meet immediately.

The naive approach of stripping non-alphanumeric characters into a new string, reversing it, and comparing works but wastes O(n) space on allocations that the two-pointer method avoids entirely. In an interview, demonstrating the in-place approach shows you understand both the algorithmic pattern and the practical concern of avoiding unnecessary allocations.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to validate printed reference codes that contained dashes and spaces for readability but required the alphanumeric core to be a palindrome under a legacy checksum rule. The two-pointer validator handled edge cases like all-separator codes and mixed-case inputs without any extra allocation, processing millions of codes in the nightly batch.

Remember one sentence: use two pointers from both ends, skip non-alphanumeric characters with a guarded inner loop, compare lowercased values, and return true if the pointers meet without a mismatch.
